title: Many tiny steps
objectives: Watch tree prices converge as the number of steps grows
Explain the odd-even sawtooth and why the leaves become lognormal

screens.title: One step, calibrated
screens.prose: A share is at £100. A one-year call is struck at £100, with $r = 5\%$ and $\sigma = 20\%$. One CRR step gives $u = e^{0.2} = 1.2214$ and $d = 1/u = 0.8187$. With growth $e^{r\Delta t}$ per step, $q = \frac{e^{0.05} - d}{u - d} = 0.5775$.
screens.question: What does the one-step tree say the call is worth?

hints.text: Only the up leaf pays. Weight it by $q$.
The payoff arrives in a year, so it must be discounted.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each payoff by its risk-neutral chance, add, then discount by $e^{-0.05}$.

byKey.no-disc: You found $0.5775 \times 22.14 = 12.79$ but did not discount it. The payoff is a year away, so multiply by $e^{-0.05}$.
byKey.old-q: You used level 1's $q = 0.625$. With these factors $q$ is 0.5775.
byKey.level1: £11.90 is level 1's tree with $u = 1.2$ and $d = 0.8$. Here the factors come from $\sigma$.
byKey.half: You weighted the leaves equally. Pricing uses the risk-neutral $q = 0.5775$, not a coin flip.

explain.text: One step is the level 1 sum with CRR factors: $e^{-0.05}(0.5775 \times 22.14) = 12.16$. This is the tree with $n = 1$. Next we cut the year into more and more steps.

screens.title: More and more steps
screens.prose: Now cut the year into $n$ steps of $\Delta t = 1/n$, with $u = e^{\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}}$ each. The dot is the $n$-step tree's price for the same call, and it leaves a trail as you slide.
screens.question: Slide $n$ from 1 up to 64. What do the tree prices do?

options.text: They zigzag, odd $n$ above and even $n$ below, and the swings shrink towards about £10.45.
They fall steadily towards zero.
options.why: You watched the drop from 1 step to 2. After that the prices climb back and settle near £10.45.

options.text: They rise steadily with $n$.
options.why: You followed the even steps, which do rise. The odd steps sit above them and fall, so the path zigzags.

options.text: They keep swinging by the same amount.
options.why: Compare the jump from 1 to 2 steps with the jump from 63 to 64. The swings shrink.

feedback.correct: The prices zigzag and close in on one value.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide slowly and compare odd and even $n$ near the end.

explain.text: Odd trees price above £10.45 and even trees below, and the gap closes as $n$ grows. At 64 steps the tree gives £10.42; at 65 it gives £10.48. Both sides meet at the dashed line.

screens.title: How fast it closes in
screens.prose: The prices **converge**: they get as close as we like to one number, £10.45, as $n$ grows. Here are even trees with $n$ a power of 2. The error is the tree price minus £10.45.
screens.question: Predict the error at 64 steps.

hints.text: Compare each error with the one above it.
From 4 to 8 steps the error goes from −0.48 to −0.24.
Each doubling halves the error: half of −0.06 is −0.03.

feedback.correct: The error halves each time $n$ doubles.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at how each error relates to the one before.

byKey.same: You kept the 32-step error. The error has halved at every doubling so far.
byKey.sign: Even trees sit below £10.45, so the error stays negative.
byKey.quarter: You halved twice. One doubling of $n$, from 32 to 64, halves it once.
byKey.zero: The tree reaches £10.45 only in the limit. At 64 steps it is still about 3p short.

explain.text: Each doubling of $n$ halves the error, so the error shrinks like $1/n$. The 64-step tree gives £10.42, an error of −£0.03. One more correct decimal place needs about ten times the steps.

screens.title: Why the sawtooth
screens.prose: Look at the leaves next to the strike. With $n = 2$ the middle leaf is exactly £100. With $n = 3$ the middle leaves are £112.24 and £89.09.
screens.question: Why do even trees price this call low and odd trees high?

options.text: An even tree puts a leaf on the strike, which pays nothing. An odd tree's nearest leaf sits above it and pays.
Odd trees have more leaves, so they add up more payoffs.
options.why: You counted leaves. A 64-step tree has more leaves than a 3-step one and prices lower, so position matters, not number.

options.text: Rounding errors grow with the number of steps.
options.why: The arithmetic is exact to many places. The swing comes from where leaves fall around £100.

options.text: Odd trees use a higher $q$.
options.why: You looked for a change in $q$. It moves smoothly with $n$, whether $n$ is odd or even.

hints.text: Where does the call's payoff bend?
The payoff has a kink at £100. Which tree has a leaf exactly there?
An even tree's middle leaf is £100 and pays £0. An odd tree's second leaf, £112.24, pays £12.24.

feedback.correct: The kink at the strike is sampled differently by odd and even trees.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the leaves closest to £100 in the two trees.

byKey.more: You counted leaves. A 64-step tree has more leaves than a 3-step one and prices lower, so position matters, not number.

explain.text: The payoff bends at £100. An even tree spends a leaf on the kink, where it pays £0, so it underprices. An odd tree's nearest leaf sits above the kink and pays, so it overprices.

screens.title: Where the leaves land
screens.prose: Each leaf of an $n$-step tree is a possible price in a year, with its risk-neutral probability. Each bar holds the probability of leaves near that price. Slide $n$ up to 128.
screens.question: What shape do the bars settle into by $n = 128$?

options.text: A peak near £100, with a short tail down to about £50 and a long tail up to about £190.
Symmetric about £100, like a normal curve.
options.why: Compare the tails: the bars are nearly empty by £50 but still visible at £180. Prices multiply, so the upside stretches further.

options.text: Flat: every price about equally likely.
options.why: The middle bars are far taller than the ends. Most paths mix ups and downs and finish near the start.

options.text: Two humps, one for up and one for down.
options.why: That is the one-step tree. With many steps the middle paths dominate.

hints.text: Slide to 128 and look at both ends of the chart.
The left tail stops near £50. How far does the right tail reach?
The bars rise to a peak near £100 and fall away more slowly to the right.

feedback.correct: The leaves pile up near £100 and spread further upwards.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide to 128 and compare the two tails.

explain.text: The leaves pile up near £100 and spread further up than down. Each step multiplies the price, so equal steps in $\ln S$ are wider in pounds going up. The dashed marks are the lognormal limit.

screens.title: The spread of log returns
screens.prose: On the tree, $\ln(S_T/S_0)$ is a sum of $n$ steps, each $+\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}$ or $-\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}$. With $\Delta t = 1/n$, each step has variance very close to $\sigma^2\Delta t$. The steps are independent.
screens.question: For large $n$, what standard deviation does $\ln(S_T/S_0)$ have? Here $\sigma = 0.2$ and $T = 1$.

widget.label: Standard deviation of the log return

hints.text: For independent steps, variances add.
$n$ steps of variance $\sigma^2/n$ each.
The total variance is $n \times 0.04/n = 0.04$. Take its square root.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the variances of the $n$ steps, then take a square root.

byKey.var: 0.04 is the variance. The standard deviation is its square root.
byKey.step: That is one step's size at $n = 128$. The sum has $n$ of them.
byKey.addsd: You added standard deviations. For independent steps you add variances, then take the root.

explain.text: Variances of independent steps add: $n \times \sigma^2\Delta t = \sigma^2 T = 0.04$, so the sd is 0.2. By the central limit theorem the sum is close to normal (limits-thm, Why sums look normal). A normal $\ln S_T$ is a lognormal $S_T$.

screens.title: One more step
screens.prose: A colleague prices the call at 16, 32 and 64 steps: £10.33, £10.39 and £10.42. Each is higher than the last. She adds one step and expects a price just above £10.42.
screens.question: What does the 65-step tree give?

options.why: You extended the rising trend of 16, 32 and 64. That trend holds for even trees; 65 is odd.
You treated one extra step as no change. Going from even to odd moves the price across the limit.
The tree reaches £10.45 only in the limit. At 65 steps it is still a few pence away.

hints.text: Is 65 odd or even?
Odd trees sat above the dashed line in the slider.
An odd tree near 64 steps is about as far above £10.45 as the even one is below.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Remember which side of £10.45 odd trees fall on.

byKey.trend: You assumed more steps always move the price up. That holds only along even $n$; 65 is odd and lands above £10.45.
byKey.nochange: You treated one extra step as no change. Going from even to odd moves the price across the limit.

explain.text: Adding one step to an even tree makes it odd, and odd trees sit above the limit. So 64 steps gives £10.42 and 65 gives £10.48. More steps shrink the error, but not from one side.

screens.title: Why the leaves are lognormal
screens.prose: Let $J$ be the number of up moves on an $n$-step tree. Each step is up with risk-neutral chance $q$, independently. We show why $S_T$ is close to lognormal.
screens.question: Put the lines of the argument in order.

lines.text: $S_T = S_0 u^J d^{\,n-J}$, since each up multiplies by $u$ and each down by $d$
$\ln(S_T/S_0) = J\ln u + (n - J)\ln d$, taking logs turns the product into a sum
$= (2J - n)\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}$, because $\ln u = \sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}$ and $\ln d = -\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}$
$J$ is a sum of $n$ independent up-or-down counts, so it is close to normal for large $n$ (central limit theorem)
$\ln(S_T/S_0)$ is a linear function of $J$, so it is close to normal: $S_T$ is close to lognormal

hints.text: Start from the price at a leaf.
Logs come before the central limit theorem: the theorem is about sums.
Price, then logs, then the CRR factors, then the normal limit for $J$, then the conclusion.

feedback.correct: Logs turn the moves into a sum, and sums become normal.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write the leaf price first, take logs, then use the central limit theorem.

byKey.s4: The central limit theorem needs a sum. Take logs first, so the moves add.
byKey.s5: That is the conclusion. It needs $J$ to be close to normal first.

explain.text: Logs turn the product of moves into a sum of moves. The central limit theorem makes that sum normal. That is the lognormal shape your bars settled into.

screens.title: Counting the work
screens.prose: A tree price touches every node once. An $n$-step tree has $k + 1$ nodes at step $k$, from the root at step 0 to $n + 1$ leaves. Write `count_nodes(n)`, the total number of nodes.

state.caption: Two steps: the middle paths meet, so step 2 has 3 nodes, not 4. Total 6.

screens.question: Complete `count_nodes(n)`.

widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests, from 0 steps to 1,000, compared exactly.

hints.text: Add the nodes step by step: $1 + 2 + \dots + (n + 1)$.
A loop over `k` in `range(n + 1)` adding `k + 1` works.
The sum is $\frac{(n + 1)(n + 2)}{2}$: return `(n + 1) * (n + 2) // 2`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Step $k$ has $k + 1$ nodes; add them for $k = 0$ to $n$.

explain.text: The total is $\frac{(n + 1)(n + 2)}{2}$, close to $n^2/2$. Doubling the steps halves the error but quadruples the work. A 500-step tree has 125,751 nodes.

screens.title: Steps on a desk
screens.prose: Desks price with a few hundred steps. Your pricer takes 2 ms for one 100-step tree. Each night the risk system revalues 5,000 options, and risk wants errors four times smaller than at 100 steps.
screens.question: How many seconds does the nightly run take with the finer tree?

hints.text: Error goes like $1/n$, work like $n^2$.
Four times smaller error needs four times the steps: 400.
Four times the steps is $4^2 = 16$ times the work: 32 ms per option, times 5,000.

feedback.correct: 400 steps cost 16 times as much: 160 seconds a night.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the steps needed first, then scale the time by the square.

byKey.linear: You scaled time with the steps. Nodes grow like $n^2$, so 4 times the steps is 16 times the work.
byKey.now: That is the run at 100 steps. The finer tree needs 400.
byKey.sqrt: You used 16 times the steps. Error goes like $1/n$, so 4 times the steps is enough.

explain.text: Four times smaller error needs 400 steps, and the work grows 16-fold to 32 ms per option. Over 5,000 options that is 160 seconds. This trade-off is why desks stop at a few hundred steps, or use a formula when one exists.

ideas: Tree prices converge to one value as the steps shrink: £10.45 for our call, the Black-Scholes price.
Odd and even trees fall on opposite sides of the limit, and the error shrinks like $1/n$, not from one side.
Log returns on the tree are sums of many small independent steps, so the leaves become lognormal.
summary.trap: One more step can move the price the other way: 64 steps gives £10.42, 65 gives £10.48.

quiz.prose: Our call is priced on trees of 100 and 101 steps.
quiz.question: Which tree prices above £10.45?

options.text: The 101-step tree
The 100-step tree
options.why: You picked the bigger round number. Even trees put a leaf on the strike and price below the limit.

options.text: Both, since 100 steps is close to the limit
options.why: Close to the limit is still on one side. Odd and even trees fall on opposite sides.

options.text: Neither: trees always underprice
options.why: Odd trees overprice this call. The 1-step tree gave £12.16.

feedback.correct: Odd trees sit above the limit here: 10.47 against 10.43.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall which side of £10.45 odd and even trees fall on.

explain.text: The 100-step tree gives £10.43 and the 101-step tree £10.47. The odd tree's leaf just above the strike pays, which overprices the call.

quiz.prose: An analyst expects the share to grow 12% a year. She argues that a 512-step tree should approach the expected payoff under 12% growth, discounted at 5%: £15.53.
quiz.question: What does the 512-step tree give?

options.why: You priced with the real-world growth. The tree uses $q$, which comes from $r$, $u$ and $d$; the 12% never enters.
That is the 12% expected payoff without discounting. The tree uses neither.
That is the 1-step tree. 512 steps is close to the limit.

feedback.correct: The tree never sees the expected growth.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which inputs the tree uses.

explain.text: The tree's $q$ depends on $r$, $\sigma$ and $\Delta t$ only. So any number of steps converges to £10.45, whatever growth anyone expects. That is replication at work: the hedge, not the forecast, sets the price.

quiz.prose: For even $n$, our call's error is about $-1.92/n$ pounds: −£0.06 at 32 steps.
quiz.question: About how many steps bring the error to −£0.01?

options.text: About 200
About 64

options.text: About 3,000
